We are given

\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n-3, & n\ge 1000,\\
f(f(n+5)), & n<1000.
\end{cases}
\]

First compute the values just below \(1000\). Since \(f(n)=n-3\) for \(n\ge 1000\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1000)&=997,\\
f(1001)&=998,\\
f(1002)&=999,\\
f(1003)&=1000,\\
f(1004)&=1001.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now use the second clause for \(n<1000\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(999)&=f(f(1004))=f(1001)=998,\\
f(998)&=f(f(1003))=f(1000)=997,\\
f(997)&=f(f(1002))=f(999)=998,\\
f(996)&=f(f(1001))=f(998)=997,\\
f(995)&=f(f(1000))=f(997)=998.
\end{aligned}
\]

So for \(995\le n\le 999\), we have

\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
997, & n \text{ even},\\
998, & n \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

In particular,

\[
f(997)=998,\qquad f(998)=997.
\]

Now suppose this parity rule has been established for all integers larger than some \(n\le 994\) and less than \(1000\). Since \(n+5\) is larger than \(n\) and still less than \(1000\), we know \(f(n+5)\).

Because adding \(5\) changes parity:

- If \(n\) is even, then \(n+5\) is odd, so \(f(n+5)=998\). Hence

  \[
  f(n)=f(f(n+5))=f(998)=997.
  \]

- If \(n\) is odd, then \(n+5\) is even, so \(f(n+5)=997\). Hence

  \[
  f(n)=f(f(n+5))=f(997)=998.
  \]

Thus the parity rule propagates downward from \(995\) to every smaller integer. Therefore, for all \(n<1000\),

\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
997, & n \text{ even},\\
998, & n \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(84\) is even,

\[
f(84)=997.
\]
